claim: There is an active feedback mechanism between the apical ECM (aECM) and the apical F-actin in tracheal cells.
source: We show that there is an active feedback mechanism between the apical ECM (aECM) and the apical F-actin in tracheal cells.
evidence: The abstract directly states this finding, which is supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript showing bidirectional effects between aECM and F-actin.

claim: Cell-cell junctions are key players in aECM patterning and organisation.
source: Furthermore, we reveal that cell-cell junctions are key players in this aECM patterning and organisation and that individual cells contribute autonomously to their aECM.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, supported by experimental data showing disruption of taenidial continuity when cell junctions are downregulated.

claim: Individual cells contribute autonomously to their aECM.
source: Furthermore, we reveal that cell-cell junctions are key players in this aECM patterning and organisation and that individual cells contribute autonomously to their aECM.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, supported by mosaic analysis experiments showing cell-autonomous contributions to taenidia.

claim: Changes in the aECM influence the levels of phosphorylated Src42A (pSrc) at cell junctions.
source: Strikingly, changes in the aECM influence the levels of phosphorylated Src42A (pSrc) at cell junctions.
evidence: The abstract states this finding, supported by experimental data showing altered pSrc levels in kkv and Blimp-1 mutants.

claim: Src42A phosphorylation levels provide a link for the ECM environment to ensure proper cytoskeletal organisation.
source: Therefore, we propose that Src42A phosphorylation levels provide a link for the ECM environment to ensure proper cytoskeletal organisation.
evidence: The abstract proposes this mechanism based on the observed relationship between aECM changes and pSrc levels, and the effects on actin organization.

claim: The ECM not only provides a passive contribution to organ shape but also impinges on the cell behaviour and genetic programmes of the organ.
source: However, increasing evidence indicates that the ECM not only provides a passive contribution to organ shape but also impinges on the cell behaviour and genetic programmes of the organ (Daley and Yamada, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Daley and Yamada, 2013.

claim: The ECM is emerging as a direct modulator of many aspects of cell biology, rather than as a mere physical network that supports cells.
source: The ECM is emerging as a direct modulator of many aspects of cell biology, rather than as a mere physical network that supports cells (Hynes, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hynes, 2014.

claim: Tracheal cells begin to secrete the components of a chitin-rich aECM that lines up the lumen of the tracheal tubes once the different branches of the tracheal system have been established.
source: Once the different branches of the tracheal system have been established to cover the overall embryonic body, tracheal cells begin to secrete the components of a chitin-rich aECM that lines up the lumen of the tracheal tubes and can be visualised by the incorporation of chitin-binding probes (Moussian et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Moussian et al., 2005.

claim: Taenidial folds are a series of cuticle ridges that compose a helical structure running perpendicular to the tube length along the entire lumen.
source: A distinctive feature of this aECM are taenidial folds, a series of cuticle ridges that compose a helical structure running perpendicular to the tube length along the entire lumen (Wigglesworth, 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wigglesworth, 1990.

claim: Taenidia are believed to confer mechanical strength to the tubes.
source: Taenidia are believed to confer mechanical strength to the tubes and have been compared to a coiled spring within a rubber tube (Thompson, 1929) or to the corrugated hose of a vacuum cleaner (Manning and Krasnow, 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Thompson, 1929 and Manning and Krasnow, 1993.

claim: Taenidia are unaffected by the presence of cell boundaries.
source: From the very first descriptions, it was noticed that taenidia are unaffected by the presence of cell boundaries (Thompson, 1929), thereby indicating that they are a supracellular structure and suggesting a substantial degree of intercellular coordination.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Thompson, 1929.

claim: Taenidial organisation correlates with that of the apical F-actin bundles in underlying cells.
source: More recently, it has been reported that taenidial organisation correlates with that of the apical F-actin bundles in underlying cells—the formation of these bundles preceding the appearance of taenidia (Matusek et al., 2006; Kondo et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Matusek et al., 2006 and Kondo et al., 2007.

claim: The formation of apical F-actin bundles precedes the appearance of taenidia.
source: More recently, it has been reported that taenidial organisation correlates with that of the apical F-actin bundles in underlying cells—the formation of these bundles preceding the appearance of taenidia (Matusek et al., 2006; Kondo et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Matusek et al., 2006 and Kondo et al., 2007.

claim: The interaction of the apical cellular membrane and the aECM determines the stability of biological tubes.
source: In addition, physical modelling has recently revealed that the interaction of the apical cellular membrane and the aECM determines the stability of biological tubes (Dong et al., 2014), thus generating more questions about how this interaction occurs.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dong et al., 2014.

claim: Taenidia began to be detectable by late stage 16 when the chitin filament was still present in the tracheal lumen.
source: Taenidia began to be detectable by late stage 16 when the chitin filament was still present in the tracheal lumen (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by direct observation in Figure 1A showing taenidia at late stage 16.

claim: Taenidia develop at the more external luminal sections, while the chitin filament lies in a central position inside the lumen.
source: Optical section analysis showed that taenidia develop at the more external luminal sections, while the chitin filament lies in a central position inside the lumen (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by optical section analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: From early stage 17, when the luminal chitin fibre is already absent, taenidia became increasingly more prominent.
source: From early stage 17, a stage when the luminal chitin fibre is already absent (Moussian et al., 2006b), taenidia became increasingly more prominent (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by observation in Figure 1E and a citation to Moussian et al., 2006b.

claim: Taenidial folds are organised as spiral rings that span many distinct cells.
source: As mentioned above, taenidial folds were organised as spiral rings that span many distinct cells (Figure 1L).
evidence: This claim is supported by observation in Figure 1L.

claim: At early stage 16, when taenidia were not yet detectable, actin rings were distinguished in the cells of the DT.
source: At early stage 16, when taenidia were not yet detectable, we distinguished some actin rings in the cells of the DT (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by observation in Figure 1G.

claim: The first actin rings to appear in the trachea were those corresponding to the fusion cells.
source: It is noteworthy that the first actin rings to appear in the trachea were those corresponding to the fusion cells, which are not related to taenidia but instead to the fusion between the lumen of adjacent segments of the DT (Lee and Kolodziej, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by observation and a citation to Lee and Kolodziej, 2002.

claim: Actin filaments and taenidia are 'in-frame'.
source: Taken together these observations, lead us to conclude that actin filaments and taenidia are 'in-frame'.
evidence: This conclusion is based on confocal microscopy and TEM observations showing co-localization of actin and taenidia.

claim: TEM images of the embryonic tracheal DT show the presence of electron dense structures in the cytoplasm underneath the taenidia that are likely to be cross-sections of actin filaments.
source: However, transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images of the embryonic tracheal DT show the presence of electron dense structures in the cytoplasm underneath the taenidia (Figure 1K, open arrow). These densities are likely to be cross-sections of actin filaments and not vesicles or microtubules because of their size.
evidence: This claim is supported by TEM images in Figure 1K and size analysis of the structures.

claim: Actin filaments are about 7 nm in diameter.
source: Whereas microtubules appear as circular structures of about 25 nm in diameter and vesicles are generally 5–20 times larger, actin filaments are only about 7 nm in diameter (Grazi, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Grazi, 1997.

claim: Alteration of the tracheal apical F-bundles by mutants in genes encoding actin polymerisation proteins causes defects in taenidial arrangement.
source: Alteration of the tracheal apical F-bundles by mutants in genes encoding actin polymerisation proteins also cause defects in taenidial arrangement (Matusek et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Matusek et al., 2006.

claim: tal/pri is essential for the formation of actin bundles that prefigure two chitin structures, namely denticles in the embryonic cuticle and taenidia in the trachea.
source: Interestingly, tal/pri is essential for the formation of actin bundles that prefigure two chitin structures, namely denticles in the embryonic cuticle and taenidia in the trachea (Kondo et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kondo et al., 2007.

claim: In most tal/pri mutant embryos, the tracheal F-actin bundles formed but they were misoriented and did not follow the ring distribution found in the wild-type.
source: In most tal/pri mutant embryos, the tracheal F-actin bundles formed but they were misoriented and did not follow the ring distribution found in the wild-type (Figure 2B,D); in some extreme cases, the bundles were completely disorganised.
evidence: This claim is supported by observations in Figure 2B and 2D.

claim: In tal/pri mutants, taenidia are organised along the same pattern as the F-actin bundles.
source: In all the cases studied, we found taenidia to be organised along the same pattern as the F-actin bundles, either running parallel to the tube axis when actin bundles were oriented in this way (Figure 2C), completely disorganised, or completely misshapen in twisted tracheal tubes when F-actin fibres were aligned in a twisted manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by observations in Figure 2C and other panels.

claim: Mutants in the gene coding for the DAAM formin disrupt tracheal actin rings and taenidia.
source: Similarly to tal/pri, mutants in the gene coding for the DAAM formin also disrupt tracheal actin rings and taenidia; this is also the case for the mutants in the gene coding for the Btk29A non-receptor tyrosine kinase, which interacts genetically with DAMM (Matusek et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations and a citation to Matusek et al., 2006.

claim: Mutants in the gene coding for the Btk29A non-receptor tyrosine kinase disrupt tracheal actin rings and taenidia.
source: Similarly to tal/pri, mutants in the gene coding for the DAAM formin also disrupt tracheal actin rings and taenidia; this is also the case for the mutants in the gene coding for the Btk29A non-receptor tyrosine kinase, which interacts genetically with DAMM (Matusek et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations and a citation to Matusek et al., 2006.

claim: Btk29A interacts genetically with DAAM.
source: Similarly to tal/pri, mutants in the gene coding for the DAAM formin also disrupt tracheal actin rings and taenidia; this is also the case for the mutants in the gene coding for the Btk29A non-receptor tyrosine kinase, which interacts genetically with DAMM (Matusek et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Matusek et al., 2006.

claim: In DAAM and Btk29A mutants, heterogeneous patterns of F-actin bundling were found in the same trachea, with stretches of perpendicular bundles followed by stretches of parallel bundles.
source: In both mutants, we found heterogeneous patterns of F-actin bundling in the same trachea, with stretches of perpendicular bundles followed by stretches of parallel bundles (Figure 2F, H).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations in Figure 2F and 2H.

claim: In DAAM and Btk29A mutants, taenidia reproduce the stretches of parallel and perpendicular orientation of the F-actin bundles.
source: In support of the close relationship between F-actin bundles and taenidia, we found the latter to reproduce the stretches of parallel and perpendicular orientation of the former (Figure 2E,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations in Figure 2E and 2G.

claim: Actin bundles were harder to observe in mutants for DAAM as they were much thinner than in the wild-type.
source: Of note, actin bundles were harder to observe in mutants for DAAM as they were much thinner than in the wild-type (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations in Figure 2F.

claim: Neither singed nor forked appear to be involved in the tracheal actin rings as these structures formed normally in sn and f mutants and also in sn;f double mutants.
source: However, neither appear to be involved in the tracheal actin rings as these structures formed normally in sn and f mutants and also in sn;f double mutants (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations of mutant phenotypes.

claim: Tracheal actin rings are not only required for proper organisation of taenidia in larvae but also appear to play an instructive role in determining their initial formation during embryonic stages.
source: All together, these results indicate that tracheal actin rings are not only required for proper organisation of taenidia in larvae (Matusek et al., 2006) but also appear to play an instructive role in determining their initial formation during embryonic stages.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations and a citation to Matusek et al., 2006.

claim: EM images have identified the accumulation of electron-dense material at the base of the taenidia that is thought to correspond to the chitin synthesis complex.
source: EM images have identified the accumulation of electron-dense material at the base of the taenidia that is thought to correspond to the chitin synthesis complex (Uv and Moussian, 2010) and that appears to be located at the top of actin fibres (Moussian et al., 2006b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Uv and Moussian, 2010 and Moussian et al., 2006b.

claim: The chitin synthesis complex appears to be located at the top of actin fibres.
source: EM images have identified the accumulation of electron-dense material at the base of the taenidia that is thought to correspond to the chitin synthesis complex (Uv and Moussian, 2010) and that appears to be located at the top of actin fibres (Moussian et al., 2006b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Moussian et al., 2006b.

claim: In the Drosophila trachea, chitin production is carried out by the membrane-inserted chitin synthase encoded by the krotzkopf verkehrt (kkv) gene.
source: In the Drosophila trachea, this production is carried out by the membrane-inserted chitin synthase encoded by the krotzkopf verkehrt (kkv) gene (Ostrowski et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ostrowski et al., 2002.

claim: The Kkv chitin synthase enzyme catalyses the linkage between N-acetyl-glucosamines supplied in the cytoplasm and extrudes the polymers across the plasma membrane.
source: The Kkv chitin synthase enzyme catalyses the linkage between N-acetyl-glucosamines supplied in the cytoplasm and extrudes the polymers across the plasma membrane (for a review see [Moussian et al., 2006b]).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Moussian et al., 2006b.

claim: A kkv-GFP-tagged construct under the control of the UAS promoter sequences rescued the tracheal phenotype of the kkv mutants when driven by the trachea-specific btlGal4 driver.
source: When driven by the trachea-specific btlGal4 driver, it rescued the tracheal phenotype of the kkv mutants (our own results and [Moussian et al., 2015]), thereby indicating that the Kkv-GFP-tagged protein is fully functional and localises properly.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and a citation to Moussian et al., 2015.

claim: KkvGFP showed a highly punctated accumulation in tracheal cells with linear arrangements perpendicular to the tube length that resembled the actin rings and chitin rings.
source: KkvGFP showed a highly punctated accumulation in tracheal cells, which makes it difficult to distinguish clear spatial patterns. However, we did detect linear arrangements perpendicular to the tube length that resembled the actin rings detected by phalloidin and the chitin rings detected by fluostain (Figure 3B and C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations in Figure 3B, 3C, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: KkvGFP dots overlap more frequently within each taenidium ring (on average, 25 dots per taenidium) compared to outside (15 dots).
source: We have quantified the number of times these KkvGFP dots overlap with the fluostain rings and observed that they are indeed more frequent within each ring (on average, 25 dots per taenidium in contrast to 15 dots outside, n = 24, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: KkvGFP dots are larger when they overlap with the fluostain rings than when they are present outside.
source: Interestingly, we also found that these KkvGFP dots are larger when they overlap with the fluostain rings than when they are present outside (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: In tal/pri mutants, Kkv dots are more aligned with the disrupted actin fibers and not in the ring arrangements observed in wild-type.
source: Interestingly, we did not observe the same arrangements upon driving kkvGFP expression in a tal/pri mutant background (100%, n = 30, Figure 3D). Instead, we found that Kkv dots are more aligned with the disrupted actin fibers.
evidence: This claim is supported by observations in Figure 3D.

claim: Blimp-1 mutant embryos were grossly inflated compared to the wild-type.
source: Indeed, Blimp-1 mutant embryos were grossly inflated compared to the wild-type (Figure 4A, B), a phenotype associated with weaker embryonic cuticles caused by mutations impairing the deposition or organisation of chitin (Ostrowski et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations in Figure 4A and 4B, and a citation to Ostrowski et al., 2002.

claim: Blimp-1 mutants showed a pale ectodermal cuticle with smaller denticles.
source: Consistent with this observation, Blimp-1 mutants showed a pale ectodermal cuticle with smaller denticles (Figure 4A, B), although their phenotype is weaker than that of the kkv chitin synthase mutants (Ostrowski et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations in Figure 4A and 4B, and a citation to Ostrowski et al., 2002.

claim: Lower levels of fluostain signal were detected in the trachea of Blimp-1 mutants compared to the wild-type.
source: In support of this hypothesis, we detected lower levels of fluostain signal in the trachea of Blimp-1 mutants compared to the wild-type (Figure 4C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations in Figure 4C and 4D.

claim: In Blimp-1 mutants, taenidia were not organised in folds perpendicular to the tube axis but instead ran parallel to it.
source: However, the most obvious abnormal feature of taenidia was their pattern, as they were not organised in folds perpendicular to the tube axis but instead ran parallel to it (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations in Figure 4F.

claim: In most Blimp-1 mutants examined (67%, n = 18), tracheal actin rings were not observed.
source: In most Blimp-1 mutants examined (67%, n = 18), we did not observe tracheal actin rings (Figure 4H, Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations in Figure 4H and Videos 1 and 2.

claim: In the Blimp-1 mutant embryos in which apical actin bundles were detected (33%, n = 18), these were oriented in parallel to the tube length.
source: However, in the mutant embryos in which we detected apical actin bundles (33%, n = 18), these were oriented in parallel to the tube length (data not shown) like the chitin structures (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: In wild-type embryos, each taenidium is formed by a plasma membrane protrusion and the taenidia have a regular shape.
source: In wild-type embryos, each taenidium is formed by a plasma membrane protrusion and the taenidia have a regular shape (Figure 5A, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by TEM observations in Figure 5A and 5D.

claim: Arrangement of plasma membrane protrusions in tal/pri and Blimp-1 mutant tracheal cells is irregular.
source: Arrangement of plasma membrane protrusions in tal/pri and Blimp-1 mutant tracheal cells is irregular (Figure 5B, C, E, F).
evidence: This claim is supported by TEM observations in Figure 5B, 5C, 5E, and 5F.

claim: At the end of embryogenesis, the breadth of taenidia is very constant in wt animals (243 nm +/-8%, n = 20), but highly variable in tal/pri mutants (346 nm, +/-35%; n = 20) and Blimp-1 mutants (543 nm +/- 45%, n =13).
source: At the end of embryogenesis, whereas the breadth of these taenidia is very constant in wt animals, it is highly variable in tal/pri and Blimp-1 mutants (wt 243 nm +/-8%, n = 20; pri 346 nm, +/-35%; n = 20 and Blimp-1 543 nm +/- 45%, n =13, measured at the basis of the taenidia contacting the plasma membrane, see 'Materials and methods' for details).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements of taenidial breadth.

claim: kkv mutants lacked actin rings.
source: Surprisingly, kkv mutants also lacked actin rings (Figure 6D), thereby indicating a feedback role of proper chitin-mediated tracheal cuticle in F-actin organisation.
evidence: This claim is supported by observations in Figure 6D.

claim: F-actin bundles formed normally and thereafter collapsed in kkv mutants.
source: In addition, F-actin bundles formed normally and thereafter collapsed in kkv mutants (Figure 6I-L, Videos 3 and 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse observations in Figure 6I-L and Videos 3 and 4.

claim: A proper cuticle is not required for the establishment of the F-actin rings but instead for their maintenance.
source: This finding indicates that a proper cuticle is not required for the establishment of the F-actin rings but instead for their maintenance.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that F-actin bundles form but then collapse in kkv mutants.

claim: Proper chitin deposition/organisation contributes to ensure the proper organisation and stability of the apical F-actin rings.
source: This implies that proper chitin deposition/organisation contributes to ensure the proper organisation and stability of the apical F-actin rings.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that F-actin rings collapse in kkv mutants.

claim: Both kkv and Blimp-1 mutations had an effect on tracheal cell shape.
source: We observed that both kkv and Blimp-1 mutations had an effect on tracheal cell shape.
evidence: This claim is supported by observations of cell shape changes in mutants.

claim: In the wild-type trachea, the cells of the DT were organised such that the longest axis of their apical shape is parallel to the tube axis.
source: In the wild-type trachea, the cells of the DT were organised such that the longest axis of their apical shape is parallel to the tube axis.
evidence: This claim is supported by observations of wild-type cell shape.

claim: In both Blimp-1 and kkv mutant trachea, the anteroposterior elongation of the cells of the DT was lost, causing cells to be more square shaped.
source: However, in both Blimp-1 and kkv mutant trachea (Figure 7B, C), the anteroposterior elongation of the cells of the DT was lost, causing cells to be more square shaped.
evidence: This claim is supported by observations in Figure 7B and 7C.

claim: A modification of cell shape/orientation occurs in embryos mutant for the Src-family kinase Src42A.
source: Interestingly, a modification of cell shape/orientation also occurs in embryos mutant for the Src-family kinase Src42A (Förster and Luschnig, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Förster and Luschnig, 2012.

claim: Taenidia follow the same organisation in Src42A mutant embryos as the wild-type.
source: However, and as previously reported for F-actin (Förster and Luschnig, 2012), we found taenidia to follow the same organisation in Src42A mutant embryos as the wild-type (Figure 7E) indicating that proper organisation of taenidia can be uncoupled from correct tracheal cell shape/orientation and thus that the former is not merely a consequence of the latter.
evidence: This claim is supported by observations in Figure 7E and a citation to Förster and Luschnig, 2012.

claim: Proper organisation of taenidia can be uncoupled from correct tracheal cell shape/orientation.
source: However, and as previously reported for F-actin (Förster and Luschnig, 2012), we found taenidia to follow the same organisation in Src42A mutant embryos as the wild-type (Figure 7E) indicating that proper organisation of taenidia can be uncoupled from correct tracheal cell shape/orientation and thus that the former is not merely a consequence of the latter.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that taenidia are properly organized in Src42A mutants despite altered cell shape.

claim: Upon expression of UASBlimp-1 under AbdB-Gal4 control, lower levels of chitin were detected in the posterior metameres.
source: Upon expression of UASBlimp-1 under these conditions, lower levels of chitin were detected in the posterior metameres (Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations in Figure 8A.

claim: Chitin deposition seems to be highly dependent on the levels of Blimp-1 activity as both loss-of-function mutations and overexpression of Blimp-1 induce low levels of chitin.
source: Thus, chitin deposition seems to be highly dependent on the levels of Blimp-1 activity as both loss-of-function mutations and overexpression of Blimp-1 induce low levels of chitin.
evidence: This claim is inferred from observations that both loss and gain of Blimp-1 function reduce chitin levels.

claim: Overexpression of Blimp-1 gives rise to tracheal cells with a less elongated apical side.
source: We also noted that overexpression of Blimp-1 gives rise to tracheal cells with a less elongated apical side (Figure 8A''), like that of Blimp-1 and kkv mutants (Figure 7B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations in Figure 8A''.

claim: Blimp-1 regulates chitin accumulation in a cell-autonomous manner.
source: Thus, we conclude that Blimp-1 regulates chitin accumulation in a cell-autonomous manner and that each cell contributes independently to the chitin deposition of their corresponding segments of the taenidial folds.
evidence: This claim is based on mosaic analysis showing cell-autonomous effects of Blimp-1 on chitin deposition.

claim: Each cell contributes independently to the chitin deposition of their corresponding segments of the taenidial folds.
source: Thus, we conclude that Blimp-1 regulates chitin accumulation in a cell-autonomous manner and that each cell contributes independently to the chitin deposition of their corresponding segments of the taenidial folds.
evidence: This claim is based on mosaic analysis showing independent contributions of cells to taenidia.

claim: Tal/Pri peptides have a non-cell autonomous function.
source: In the case of the tal/pri rescue experiment, we detected a difference between the cells expressing the wild-type tal/pri gene and those with a wild-type phenotype, an observation consistent with the non-cell autonomous function of the Tal/Pri peptides (Kondo et al., 2007; Galindo et al., 2007; Chanut-Delalande et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations and citations to Kondo et al., 2007; Galindo et al., 2007; Chanut-Delalande et al., 2014.

claim: In the Blimp-1 rescue experiment, taenidia tended to follow the orientation dictated by the genotype of their respective cells.
source: However, in the case of the Blimp-1 rescue experiment, taenidia tended to follow the orientation dictated by the genotype of their respective cells (Figure 8D and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations in Figure 8D and 8F.

claim: Tracheal taenidia can form proper rings even when the neighbouring cells do not.
source: These results show that tracheal taenidia can form proper rings even when the neighbouring cells do not.
evidence: This claim is based on mosaic analysis observations.

claim: Segments of taenidia can organise properly even in the absence of proper subjacent actin rings provided that the segments of taenidia contributed by the neighbouring cells are properly organised.
source: This indicates that, to a certain degree, segments of taenidia can organise properly even in the absence of proper subjacent actin rings provided that the segments of taenidia contributed by the neighbouring cells are properly organised.
evidence: This claim is inferred from mosaic analysis observations.

claim: Upon expression of a dsRNA targeted at the gene encoding alpha-catenin (α-cat), DE-cad was strongly downregulated (undetected by antibody staining), demonstrating that adherens junction (AJ) formation is disrupted in the DT.
source: Upon expression of a dsRNA targeted at the gene encoding alpha-catenin (α-cat), we found that DE-cad was strongly downregulated (undetected by antibody staining), demonstrating that adherens junction (AJ) formation is disrupted in the DT of these embryos (Figure 9—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations in Figure 9—figure supplement 1H.

claim: By downregulating AJs, taenidia organised in groups of independent units, not encompassing the overall tracheal tube diameter.
source: By downregulating AJs, we found that in these embryos taenidia organised in groups of independent units, not encompassing the overall tracheal tube diameter (Figure 9 B) (cell-cell junction taenidial disruption was detected in 123 out of 156 DT cells analysed (79%), n = 18 larvae).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations in Figure 9B.

claim: Despite the observed role of cell-cell junctions in taenidial continuity, taenidia are still placed perpendicular to the tube length when junctions are disrupted.
source: Strikingly, despite the observed role of cell-cell junctions in taenidial continuity, these are still placed perpendicular to the tube length.
evidence: This claim is based on observations of taenidial orientation in α-cat RNAi experiments.

claim: Tracheal cells are able to sense a global orientation cue and align their actin bundles appropriately despite having their continuity disrupted at the level of the cell-cell junctions.
source: This suggests that tracheal cells are able to sense a global orientation cue and align their actin bundles appropriately (Matusek et al., 2006), despite having their continuity disrupted at the level of the cell-cell junctions.
evidence: This claim is inferred from observations and supported by a citation to Matusek et al., 2006.

claim: In the α-cat RNAi mutant background, taenidia organisation mimicked the distribution of actin bundles, which were similarly restricted to independent units (100%, n = 17 larvae).
source: Also, in this mutant background, taenidia organisation mimicked the distribution of actin bundles (Figure 9—figure supplement 1), which were similarly restricted to these independent units (100%, n = 17 larvae).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: Double labelling with fluostain and an apical cell membrane marker showed that the independent taenidial units corresponded to single cells.
source: Double labelling these trachea with fluostain and an apical cell membrane marker showed that these units corresponded to single cells (Figure 9B and C), thereby confirming the role of cell-junctions in coordinating the pattern of F-actin bundles from neighbouring tracheal cells and ensuring a supracellular taenidia organisation encompassing the overall tracheal tube.
evidence: This claim is supported by observations in Figure 9B and 9C.

claim: Cell-junctions play a role in coordinating the pattern of F-actin bundles from neighbouring tracheal cells and ensuring a supracellular taenidia organisation encompassing the overall tracheal tube.
source: Double labelling these trachea with fluostain and an apical cell membrane marker showed that these units corresponded to single cells (Figure 9B and C), thereby confirming the role of cell-junctions in coordinating the pattern of F-actin bundles from neighbouring tracheal cells and ensuring a supracellular taenidia organisation encompassing the overall tracheal tube.
evidence: This claim is based on observations from α-cat RNAi experiments.

claim: Higher levels of Src42A phosphorylation were observed in kkv and Blimp-1 mutants.
source: We observed higher levels of Src42A phosphorylation in kkv and Blimp-1 mutants (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations.

claim: In the trachea, increased levels of Src42A phosphorylation have been shown to be coupled to an enhanced Src42A activity.
source: In the trachea, these increased levels have been shown to be coupled to an enhanced Src42A activity (Förster and Luschnig, 2012; Nelson et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Förster and Luschnig, 2012 and Nelson et al., 2012.

claim: In all cases where kkv expression was downregulated at the posterior tracheal metameres (n = 4), there was an increased level of phosphorylated Src42A in those metameres.
source: Although the kkv RNAi inactivation appeared to be highly inefficient in this context as we obtained very few embryos with lower levels of chitin at their posterior tracheal metameres, in all these cases (n = 4) there was an increased level of phosphorylated Src42A in the metameres where kkv expression was downregulated (Figure 10A, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations in Figure 10A and 10D.

claim: There was a difference in levels of phosphorylated Src42A between kkv mutant and kkv-rescued cells.
source: This observation was confirmed by the difference in levels of phosphorylated Src42A between kkv mutant and kkv-rescued cells (Figure 10C, F).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations in Figure 10C and 10F.

claim: Lower levels of phosphorylated Src42A were detected in regions with higher chitin levels upon Blimp-1 rescue of the posterior tracheal region of Blimp-1 mutant embryos.
source: In addition, lower levels of phosphorylated Src42A were detected in regions with higher chitin levels upon Blimp-1 rescue of the posterior tracheal region of Blimp-1 mutant embryos (Figure 10B, E).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations in Figure 10B and 10E.

claim: No differences in Src protein levels were detected in kkv mutant cells.
source: To check whether these differences could be attributed to differences in overall Src protein levels, we analysed Src protein in kkv mutant embryos and in embryos where Kkv was downregulated at the posterior end. In all cases, we could not detect any differences in Src protein levels in kkv mutant cells (Figure 10—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations in Figure 10—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: There is no cross-reactivity of anti-pSrc (pY418) with other phosphorylated proteins in the embryo.
source: Furthermore, we checked for the anti-pSrc (pY418) specificity in Src42A mutants and confirmed that there is no cross-reactivity with other phosphorylated proteins in the embryo (Figure 10—figure supplement 1A–D) (Förster and Luschnig, 2012; Shindo et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations in Figure 10—figure supplement 1A–D and citations to Förster and Luschnig, 2012 and Shindo et al., 2008.

claim: Downregulation of chitin synthesis leads to an increased phosphorylation of Src42A.
source: Thus, given that downregulation of chitin synthesis leads to an increased phosphorylation of Src42A (Figure 9A-C) and that an increased activity of Src42A disturbs actin bundling (Förster and Luschnig, 2012), we propose that Src42A is one of the mediators of the extracellular chitin matrix in ensuring actin bundle organisation.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations and a citation to Förster and Luschnig, 2012.

claim: An increased activity of Src42A disturbs actin bundling.
source: Thus, given that downregulation of chitin synthesis leads to an increased phosphorylation of Src42A (Figure 9A-C) and that an increased activity of Src42A disturbs actin bundling (Förster and Luschnig, 2012), we propose that Src42A is one of the mediators of the extracellular chitin matrix in ensuring actin bundle organisation.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Förster and Luschnig, 2012.

claim: Src42A is one of the mediators of the extracellular chitin matrix in ensuring actin bundle organisation.
source: Thus, given that downregulation of chitin synthesis leads to an increased phosphorylation of Src42A (Figure 9A-C) and that an increased activity of Src42A disturbs actin bundling (Förster and Luschnig, 2012), we propose that Src42A is one of the mediators of the extracellular chitin matrix in ensuring actin bundle organisation.
evidence: This claim is proposed based on experimental observations and inference.

claim: Taenidia are normally organised in Src42A loss-of-function mutants indicating that the wild-type function of Src42A is not an absolute requirement for the wild-type taenidial patterning.
source: Of note and as mentioned above, while constitutive non-regulated activity of Src42A is sufficient to disturb taenidia, taenidia are normally organised in Src42A loss-of-function mutants indicating that the wild-type function of Src42A is not an absolute requirement for the wild-type taenidial patterning.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations of Src42A mutants.

claim: No actin ring phenotype was detected in the trachea of double mutant embryos for both Src42A and Src64B.
source: However, we did not detect any actin ring phenotype in the trachea of double mutant embryos for both Src42A and Src64B (Figure 7G).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations in Figure 7G.

claim: The feedback mechanism of the chitin aECM through Src42A is not mainly in instructing actin ring organisation but in preventing its disturbance by downregulating Src42A phosphorylation to levels compatible with proper actin ring organisation.
source: Thus, and irrespective of the nature of the role of Src42A activity on actin ring patterning, these results suggest that the feedback mechanism of the chitin aECM through Src42A is not mainly in instructing actin ring organisation but in preventing its disturbance by downregulating Src42A phosphorylation to levels compatible with proper actin ring organisation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that Src42A loss-of-function does not affect taenidia but increased activity does.

claim: Genetic removal of Src42A in Blimp-1 homozygous embryos rescues the taenidial organisation phenotype to wild-type levels, while keeping other Blimp-1 mutant features in all double mutant embryos observed (n = 12).
source: Accordingly, genetic removal of Src42A in Blimp-1 homozygous embryos, rescues the taenidial organisation phenotype to wild-type levels, while keeping other Blimp-1 mutant features in all double mutant embryos observed (n = 12, Figure 10G-I), confirming the biological role of Src42A in the mechanism underlying the supracellular organisation of the tracheal aECM.
evidence: This claim is supported by observations in Figure 10G-I.

claim: Actin polymerises in rings at the apical side of the tracheal cells in a tal/pri-dependent process.
source: On the one hand, actin polymerises in rings at the apical side of the tracheal cells in a tal/pri-dependent process; these actin rings are then required for the particular accumulation of the kkv chitin synthase and for the appearance of folds in the plasma membrane.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Actin rings are required for the particular accumulation of the kkv chitin synthase and for the appearance of folds in the plasma membrane.
source: On the one hand, actin polymerises in rings at the apical side of the tracheal cells in a tal/pri-dependent process; these actin rings are then required for the particular accumulation of the kkv chitin synthase and for the appearance of folds in the plasma membrane.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations showing Kkv distribution patterns and membrane fold formation.

claim: Kkv accumulation leads to a localised increased production and deposition of chitin along specific enriched stripes above the actin rings in a Blimp-1-mediated process.
source: In turn, kkv accumulation leads to a localised increased production and deposition of chitin along specific enriched stripes above the actin rings in a Blimp-1-mediated process.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations of Kkv localization and chitin deposition patterns.

claim: The cellular AJs are instrumental in ensuring that apical F-actin bundles from each cell follow a supracellular organ arrangement.
source: On the other hand, the cellular AJs are instrumental in ensuring that apical F-actin bundles from each cell follow a supracellular organ arrangement.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations from α-cat RNAi experiments.

claim: Each cell appears to independently organise or maintain, to a certain degree, the proper orientation of their actin bundles.
source: It has to be noted that each cell appears to independently organise or maintain, to a certain degree, the proper orientation of their actin bundles, as determined by Blimp-1 clonal analysis and the disruption of cell adhesion by downregulation of α-Cat and, consequently, DE-Cad.
evidence: This claim is based on mosaic analysis and cell adhesion disruption experiments.

claim: Cells have the capacity to modify the orientation of their sections of the taenidia to keep the continuity of these structures along the tube.
source: Nevertheless, this is not an absolute value as cells also have the capacity to modify the orientation of their sections of the taenidia to keep the continuity of these structures along the tube.
evidence: This claim is based on observations of intermediate taenidial orientations in mosaic experiments.

claim: Cell adhesion is central to ensure the continuity of the intracellular actin bundles as a patterning element for the overall tube.
source: In this regard, cell adhesion is central to ensure the continuity of the intracellular actin bundles as a patterning element for the overall tube.
evidence: This claim is based on observations from cell adhesion disruption experiments.

claim: The chitin aECM feeds back on to the cellular architecture by stabilising F-actin bundling and cell shape via the modulation of Src42A phosphorylation levels.
source: Subsequently, the chitin aECM feeds back on to the cellular architecture by stabilising F-actin bundling and cell shape via the modulation of Src42A phosphorylation levels.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations showing the relationship between chitin, pSrc levels, and actin organization.

claim: A transient chitin filament is formed inside the tracheal lumen prior to taenidial fold formation.
source: It is worth mentioning that, prior to taenidial fold formation, a transient chitin filament is formed inside the tracheal lumen.
evidence: This claim is based on observations of chitin structures during development.

claim: The transient chitin filament has been postulated to regulate tube length and diameter expansion.
source: This filament has been postulated to regulate tube length and diameter expansion (Tonning et al., 2005; Moussian et al., 2006a; Luschnig and Uv, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tonning et al., 2005; Moussian et al., 2006a; Luschnig and Uv, 2014.

claim: Constitutively active mutations of Src42A disturb tracheal actin bundling.
source: In particular, constitutively active mutations of Src42A disturb tracheal actin bundling (Förster and Luschnig, 2012) and, consequently, taenidial formation (Figure 7 F).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations in Figure 7F and a citation to Förster and Luschnig, 2012.

claim: Constitutively active mutations of Src42A disturb taenidial formation.
source: In particular, constitutively active mutations of Src42A disturb tracheal actin bundling (Förster and Luschnig, 2012) and, consequently, taenidial formation (Figure 7 F).
evidence: This claim is supported by observations in Figure 7F.

claim: Blimp-1 is an ecdysone response gene.
source: Thus, we turned to Blimp-1, an ecdysone response gene (Chavoshi et al., 2010; Beckstead et al., 2005) that encodes the Drosophila homolog of the transcriptional factor B-lymphocyte-inducing maturation protein gene and whose mutants have been reported to have misshapen trachea almost completely devoid of taenidia (Ng et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chavoshi et al., 2010 and Beckstead et al., 2005.

claim: Blimp-1 encodes the Drosophila homolog of the transcriptional factor B-lymphocyte-inducing maturation protein gene.
source: Thus, we turned to Blimp-1, an ecdysone response gene (Chavoshi et al., 2010; Beckstead et al., 2005) that encodes the Drosophila homolog of the transcriptional factor B-lymphocyte-inducing maturation protein gene and whose mutants have been reported to have misshapen trachea almost completely devoid of taenidia (Ng et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.
